etl.plain: A data pipeline is a repeatable program that copies data from where it is created to where it can be analyzed. ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load: you pull data out of a source system, clean and reshape it, then load it into a destination such as a data warehouse (a database built for analysis over large tables). ELT swaps the last two steps: you load the raw data first and do the cleaning inside the warehouse. Either way, the goal is a small set of trusted, well-named tables that dashboards, machine learning models and AI agents can rely on.
etl.analogy: Think of a restaurant receiving deliveries. The raw crates go into the walk-in fridge exactly as they arrived (the raw layer), cooks then wash, chop and portion them (transform), and only plated dishes go out to diners (the marts).
etl.why: Almost every customer engagement starts with scattered data: an ERP in Oracle, a CRM in Salesforce, and a folder of CSV exports someone emails every Monday. Before an FDE can build a claims assistant for an insurer or a forecasting tool for a retailer, that data has to arrive daily, correctly and without duplicates. If the pipeline is shaky, every product built on top of it inherits the errors.

subtopics.title: Extracting: full loads and watermarks
subtopics.body:
Extraction means reading data out of a source system. The first time, you usually do a full load: copy every row. That is fine once, but copying a 200 million row table every night is slow and puts load on the customer's production database.

After the first load you switch to incremental extraction. The most common method is a watermark: a column such as updated_at that tells you when each row last changed. You remember the highest value you have already copied, and next time you only ask for rows newer than that.

A stronger option is change data capture (CDC). CDC reads the database's own transaction log, so it also sees deletes, which a watermark query cannot. Tools such as Debezium or a cloud provider's replication service do this for you.
subtopics.example: A retailer, Northwind Stores, keeps orders in PostgreSQL. On day one you copy all 12 million orders. You store the watermark 2026-03-01 23:59:58. The next night you ask only for orders with updated_at greater than that value and receive 41,300 rows in a few seconds. You save the new watermark only after the load succeeds, so a failed run simply retries the same window.
subtopics.code:
import json, pathlib
import psycopg  # psycopg 3

STATE = pathlib.Path("state/orders_watermark.json")

def read_watermark() -> str:
    # Default to the start of time on the very first (full) load
    if STATE.exists():
        return json.loads(STATE.read_text())["updated_at"]
    return "1970-01-01T00:00:00"

def extract_orders(conn_str: str):
    wm = read_watermark()
    with psycopg.connect(conn_str) as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at > %s ORDER BY updated_at",
            (wm,),  # parameterized, never string-formatted
        ).fetchall()
    return rows, wm

def save_watermark(new_wm: str) -> None:
    # Call this only AFTER the load step succeeded
    STATE.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    STATE.write_text(json.dumps({"updated_at": new_wm}))

subtopics.title: Landing raw data in layers
subtopics.body:
In ELT you save exactly what you extracted, unchanged, before doing anything else. This raw copy is your safety net. If a transformation has a bug, you fix the code and rerun it over the raw data instead of asking the customer for another export.

Many teams name their layers with the medallion pattern. Bronze holds raw data as it landed. Silver holds cleaned data with correct types and no duplicates. Gold holds business-ready tables, often called marts, organized around topics such as orders or claims.

Raw data is commonly stored as Parquet files, a compressed column-based file format, split into folders by date. Splitting data into folders like this is called partitioning, and it lets later jobs read only the days they need.
subtopics.example: An insurer, Harbor Mutual, sends a nightly claims extract. You write it to bronze/claims/load_date=2026-03-02/part-0.parquet. Two weeks later you discover the claim_amount column was parsed as text. You fix the silver transformation and rebuild 14 days of silver data from bronze in minutes, without touching the insurer's systems.
subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd
from datetime import date

def land_raw(rows: list[dict], table: str, lake_root: str = "lake") -> str:
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["_loaded_at"] = pd.Timestamp.utcnow()      # audit column
    load_date = date.today().isoformat()
    path = f"{lake_root}/bronze/{table}/load_date={load_date}"
    # One folder per day = one partition. Rerunning overwrites that day only.
    df.to_parquet(f"{path}/part-0.parquet", index=False)  # needs pyarrow
    return path

# land_raw(rows, "claims")
# -> lake/bronze/claims/load_date=2026-03-02/part-0.parquet

subtopics.title: Transforming with SQL
subtopics.body:
Transformation turns raw rows into clean ones. Typical jobs are: fixing data types, renaming cryptic columns, removing duplicates, standardizing values such as country codes, and joining tables together.

Most modern teams write transformations in SQL and run them inside the warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift or Postgres). A tool called dbt lets you keep each transformation as a SQL file in git, with tests and documentation, and runs them in the right order.

Deduplication is the transformation you will write most often. Source systems and incremental loads both produce repeated rows. The standard trick is ROW_NUMBER(): number the copies of each record from newest to oldest and keep number one.
subtopics.example: Northwind's bronze orders table has 3 copies of order 88213 because the order was edited twice. The query below keeps only the newest version per order_id, casts the amount from text to a decimal, and upper-cases the country code so 'us', 'US ' and 'Us' all become 'US'.
subtopics.code:
-- silver.orders: one clean row per order
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE silver.orders AS
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(12,2))      AS amount,
    UPPER(TRIM(country_code))          AS country_code,
    CAST(updated_at AS TIMESTAMP)      AS updated_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id            -- one group per order
      ORDER BY updated_at DESC         -- newest version first
    ) AS rn
  FROM bronze.orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, country_code, updated_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;                          -- keep only the newest copy

subtopics.title: Idempotent loads with MERGE
subtopics.body:
A job is idempotent when running it twice gives the same result as running it once. Pipelines fail and get retried all the time, so this property matters a lot.

The classic mistake is a plain INSERT that appends rows. If the job crashes after inserting half the rows and then retries, you get duplicates. Revenue dashboards then show numbers that are too high, and nobody notices for weeks.

Two safe patterns exist. The first is to overwrite a whole partition, for example delete and rewrite all of March 2nd. The second is MERGE, sometimes called an upsert: for each incoming row, update it if the key already exists, insert it if it does not.
subtopics.example: A hospital network, Riverside Health, loads 9,000 appointment updates per night. The job fails at 2 a.m. after writing 5,000 rows. With MERGE on appointment_id, the retry updates those 5,000 in place and inserts the remaining 4,000. The table ends with exactly 9,000 changed rows either way.
subtopics.code:
MERGE INTO gold.appointments AS target
USING silver.appointments_today AS src
  ON target.appointment_id = src.appointment_id   -- the business key
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
  status       = src.status,
  scheduled_at = src.scheduled_at,
  updated_at   = src.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
  (appointment_id, patient_id, status, scheduled_at, updated_at)
VALUES
  (src.appointment_id, src.patient_id, src.status,
   src.scheduled_at, src.updated_at);
-- Running this twice leaves the table in the same state.

subtopics.title: Data quality tests and freshness
subtopics.body:
Data quality tests are small checks that run after each transformation. They catch problems before a business user or an AI agent sees them.

Start with four kinds. Not-null checks that required columns are filled. Uniqueness checks that keys appear once. Referential integrity checks that every foreign key points to a real row, for example every order's customer_id exists in customers. Freshness checks that the newest row is recent enough, so a stalled pipeline raises an alert instead of silently serving old data.

In dbt you declare these tests in a YAML file next to your models. A failing test stops downstream models from building, which is exactly what you want.
subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's claims assistant answers 'What is the status of claim C-55120?'. One Monday the extract job silently stopped, and the assistant kept answering from Friday's data. A freshness rule that warns after 12 hours and errors after 24 hours would have paged the on-call engineer on Saturday morning.
subtopics.code:
# models/schema.yml (dbt). Recent dbt versions call the key data_tests;
# older versions use tests.
version: 2
sources:
  - name: bronze
    tables:
      - name: claims
        loaded_at_field: _loaded_at
        freshness:
          warn_after:  {count: 12, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
models:
  - name: claims
    columns:
      - name: claim_id
        data_tests: [not_null, unique]
      - name: policy_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:          # every claim points at a real policy
              to: ref('policies')
              field: policy_id

subtopics.title: Orchestrating the whole pipeline
subtopics.body:
An orchestrator is a scheduler that runs the steps of a pipeline in order, retries failures and shows you what happened. Apache Airflow is the most common one. Dagster and Prefect are popular alternatives, and cloud warehouses have their own simpler schedulers.

In Airflow a pipeline is a DAG, short for directed acyclic graph: a set of tasks with arrows showing which must finish before which, and no loops. You write it in Python. Each task should be small and idempotent so a retry is safe.

When choosing ETL versus ELT, ask where sensitive data may land. If regulations say patient names must be masked before they leave the hospital's network, you transform first (ETL). Otherwise ELT is usually simpler and keeps a replayable raw copy.
subtopics.example: For Northwind the daily DAG runs at 02:00: extract orders, land them in bronze, run dbt to build silver and gold, run dbt tests, then notify a Slack channel. If extract fails, Airflow retries it three times, five minutes apart, and the downstream tasks wait.

glossary: Data warehouse
A database designed for analytical queries over large tables, such as Snowflake, BigQuery or Redshift.
Watermark
A stored value, often a timestamp, marking how far an incremental extract has already read.
Change data capture (CDC)
Reading a database's transaction log to capture every insert, update and delete as it happens.
Partition
A slice of a table or dataset, usually by date, stored separately so jobs can read or overwrite just that slice.
Idempotent
Safe to run more than once: repeating the job gives the same end result.
MERGE (upsert)
A SQL statement that updates rows whose key already exists and inserts rows whose key does not.
Medallion layers
A naming pattern of bronze (raw), silver (cleaned) and gold (business-ready) data.
dbt
A tool that manages SQL transformations as version-controlled files with tests and dependency ordering.
DAG
Directed acyclic graph: a set of tasks with ordering arrows and no cycles, used by orchestrators like Airflow.
practice: Download any public CSV (for example a city's open data on permits), load it into a local DuckDB or SQLite file as a raw table, then write one SQL query that deduplicates it with ROW_NUMBER(). Deliverable: the raw table, the clean table and a row count for each.

Write a Python script that extracts rows newer than a stored watermark from a SQLite table, saves them to a date-partitioned Parquet folder and updates the watermark only on success. Deliverable: run it twice in a row and show that the second run extracts zero new rows.

Stretch: build a three-task Airflow DAG (or a Dagster job) that extracts, transforms with MERGE, and runs a not-null plus uniqueness check that fails the run on bad data. Deliverable: a screenshot of one green run and one run that correctly fails after you insert a duplicate key.

fastapi.plain: FastAPI is a Python framework for building web APIs, which are programs that other programs talk to over HTTP (the protocol your browser uses). You write ordinary Python functions and attach them to URLs such as POST /ask, and FastAPI handles reading the request, checking its data and turning your return value into JSON. It uses Pydantic, a library that validates data against Python type hints, so bad input is rejected with a clear error before your code runs. It also generates interactive documentation at /docs automatically.
fastapi.analogy: FastAPI is like the front desk of a hotel. It checks every guest's booking details against a form (validation), checks their ID (authentication), then sends them to the right room (your function), and hands back a neatly printed receipt (the JSON response).
fastapi.why: Most FDE prototypes become a service that the customer's other systems must call: a claims summarizer behind the insurer's portal, or a search endpoint for a bank's internal tools. FastAPI lets you ship that quickly with input validation and docs the customer's engineers can read. When it slows down under real traffic, you need to know how its request pipeline works to find out why.

subtopics.title: Your first endpoint
subtopics.body:
An endpoint is a combination of an HTTP method (GET to read, POST to create or submit, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove) and a path such as /orders/{order_id}.

In FastAPI you create an app object, then decorate a function with the method and path. Parts of the path in curly braces become path parameters. Function arguments that are not in the path become query parameters, the key=value pairs after a question mark in a URL.

Type hints do real work here. If you declare order_id: int and a client sends /orders/abc, FastAPI returns a 422 error saying the value is not a valid integer. You run the app with Uvicorn, an ASGI server (ASGI is the standard interface between Python async web apps and servers).
subtopics.example: A logistics company, Crestline Freight, wants a quick way to look up shipments. GET /shipments/7731?include_events=true returns the shipment and its tracking events. GET /shipments/hello returns a 422 before any database is touched.

subtopics.title: Request and response models
subtopics.body:
For POST requests the client sends a JSON body. You describe the expected shape with a Pydantic model: a class that inherits from BaseModel and lists fields with types. Field() adds rules such as minimum length or allowed ranges.

FastAPI parses the JSON into that model. If a field is missing, has the wrong type or breaks a rule, the client gets a 422 response listing each problem by field name. Your function never sees bad data.

The response_model argument does the same on the way out. It validates what you return and drops any field not declared in the model. This protects you from accidentally leaking internal fields such as a customer's internal risk score.
subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's portal sends {"claim_id": "C-55120", "question": "Why was this denied?"}. If the portal sends question: "" the API answers 422 with the message that the string should have at least 3 characters. The response includes answer and sources, and the internal fields token_count and raw_prompt are stripped out.

subtopics.title: Dependencies for auth and database sessions
subtopics.body:
Many endpoints need the same setup: check the caller's token, open a database connection, load settings. FastAPI handles this with dependencies. You write a function and ask for it with Depends(). FastAPI calls it before your endpoint and passes in the result.

A dependency can use yield. Code before yield runs before the request, code after yield runs after the response, which is perfect for opening and closing a database session.

If a dependency raises HTTPException(401), the endpoint never runs. You can attach a dependency to a whole router so every route is protected without repeating yourself.
subtopics.example: A bank's internal tool requires an API key in the X-API-Key header. The require_key dependency checks it against a set loaded from the environment. Requests without it get 401. Every route under /v1 is protected by one line on the router.

subtopics.title: async def versus def
subtopics.body:
FastAPI runs on an event loop: a single thread that switches between many requests whenever one of them is waiting for I/O (a network call, a database query, a file read). An async def function signals that it will await such operations and give the loop a chance to serve others.

The danger is calling something slow and blocking inside async def, for example requests.get() or a synchronous database driver. That call holds the event loop, so every other request on that worker waits too. CPU stays low but latency climbs.

The rules are simple. Inside async def, use async libraries such as httpx.AsyncClient and await them. If you must call a blocking library, either declare the endpoint with plain def (FastAPI then runs it in a thread pool) or wrap the call with run_in_threadpool.
subtopics.example: Crestline's service calls a slow carrier API that takes 2 seconds. With requests.get inside async def, 50 concurrent users on one worker are served one after another, so the last waits about 100 seconds. Switching to await httpx.AsyncClient().get(...) lets all 50 wait at the same time and each finishes in about 2 seconds.

subtopics.title: Streaming LLM answers
subtopics.body:
A language model can take 10 to 30 seconds to write a long answer. If the API waits for the whole answer, users stare at a spinner. Streaming sends pieces of text to the client as soon as the model produces them.

In FastAPI you return a StreamingResponse wrapping an async generator, a function that uses yield to hand out chunks one at a time. The Anthropic Python SDK offers messages.stream(), which gives you a text_stream you can iterate over.

Server-sent events (SSE) is a simple format for streaming text over HTTP that browsers understand natively. Each chunk is a line starting with data: followed by a blank line.
subtopics.example: A hospital's discharge-summary assistant writes about 600 words. Without streaming, nurses wait around 20 seconds. With streaming, the first words appear in under a second and the rest arrive as they are generated, which makes the tool feel usable on a busy ward.
subtopics.code:
import json
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
llm = AsyncAnthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
MODEL = "MODEL"                 # placeholder model name

class Prompt(BaseModel):
    question: str

@app.post("/ask/stream")
async def ask_stream(body: Prompt):
    async def events():
        async with llm.messages.stream(
            model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body.question}],
        ) as stream:
            async for text in stream.text_stream:          # chunks as they arrive
                yield f"data: {json.dumps({'text': text})}\n\n"   # SSE format
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream")

subtopics.title: Testing with TestClient and overrides
subtopics.body:
FastAPI ships a TestClient that calls your app in memory, without starting a server. You write normal pytest functions that send requests and check status codes and JSON.

The most useful testing feature is app.dependency_overrides. It lets you swap a real dependency, such as the auth check or the database session, for a fake one during tests. You can test your endpoint logic without real credentials or a real database.

Good tests for an API cover the happy path, a validation failure (422), an auth failure (401) and a not-found case (404). These are the cases a customer's integration team will hit first.
subtopics.example: Before handing the bank's API to their team, you write four tests. One checks that a valid key and account returns 200. One checks that a missing header gives 422 (the header is required). One checks that a wrong key gives 401. One overrides the database with a fake that returns nothing and checks for 404.
subtopics.code:
# test_api.py   run with:  pytest -q
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app, require_key

client = TestClient(app)

def test_rejects_bad_key():
    r = client.get("/v1/accounts/1", headers={"X-API-Key": "nope"})
    assert r.status_code == 401

def test_missing_header_is_422():
    r = client.get("/v1/accounts/1")
    assert r.status_code == 422

def test_with_auth_overridden():
    app.dependency_overrides[require_key] = lambda: "test-key"  # skip real auth
    try:
        r = client.get("/v1/accounts/1")
        assert r.status_code in (200, 404)
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.clear()

glossary: API
Application programming interface: a defined way for one program to request data or actions from another.
Endpoint
One HTTP method plus path, such as POST /ask, handled by one function.
Pydantic
A Python library that validates and parses data using type hints; FastAPI uses it for requests and responses.
422 Unprocessable Entity
The status code FastAPI returns when request data fails validation.
Dependency injection
Declaring what a function needs (auth, DB session) and letting the framework supply it.
ASGI
Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: the standard connecting async Python apps to servers like Uvicorn.
Event loop
The single thread that runs async code, switching between tasks whenever one awaits I/O.
Server-sent events (SSE)
A simple HTTP format for a server to push a stream of text messages to a client.
practice: Build a FastAPI app with GET /items/{item_id} and POST /items using a Pydantic model with at least one Field rule. Deliverable: screenshots from /docs showing one 200 response and one 422 response.
Add an API-key dependency to a router, then write four pytest tests (200, 401, 404, 422) using TestClient and dependency_overrides. Deliverable: a passing pytest -q output.

Stretch: create two endpoints that each wait on a 2-second external call, one using requests inside async def and one using httpx.AsyncClient. Load test both with 20 concurrent requests (for example with the hey or oha tool). Deliverable: a short table comparing total time and explaining the difference.

deploy.plain: Deploying means getting your code running on servers where users can reach it. Docker packages your app and everything it needs (Python version, libraries, files) into an image, a single file-like bundle that runs the same way on any machine. A running copy of an image is called a container. Kubernetes is a system that runs many containers across a group of servers, called a cluster, restarts them when they crash, and spreads traffic across them.
deploy.analogy: A Docker image is like a sealed meal kit with every ingredient and the recipe card inside, so any kitchen can cook the same dish. Kubernetes is the restaurant manager who makes sure three cooks are always working, replaces one who goes home sick, and seats customers at whichever station is free.
deploy.why: An FDE's work only counts once it runs in the customer's environment, often their own cloud account or data center with strict security rules. A bank will ask how you roll back a bad release, where secrets are stored and what happens if a server dies. Containers and Kubernetes give standard answers to each of those questions.

subtopics.title: Images, containers and registries
subtopics.body:
An image is a read-only template built from a recipe file called a Dockerfile. A container is a running process started from that image, isolated from other processes on the same machine. You can start many containers from one image.

Images are built in layers. Each instruction in the Dockerfile creates a layer, and Docker caches layers that have not changed, so rebuilding after a small code edit is fast.

A registry is a server that stores images, similar to how GitHub stores code. Docker Hub is public. Customers usually have private ones such as AWS ECR, Azure ACR or Google Artifact Registry. Every image gets a tag, a label such as 1.4.2. Always use a specific version tag so you know exactly what is running.
subtopics.example: You build the image for Harbor Mutual's claims API, tag it 1.4.2 and push it to the insurer's private ECR registry. Their Kubernetes cluster pulls 1.4.2 from there. If 1.4.3 misbehaves, they can point back at 1.4.2, which is still stored unchanged.
subtopics.code:
# Build an image from the Dockerfile in the current folder
docker build -t claims-api:1.4.2 .

# Run it locally, mapping container port 8000 to your laptop's port 8000
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env claims-api:1.4.2

# See running containers and their logs
docker ps
docker logs <container_id>

# Tag for the customer's registry and push
docker tag claims-api:1.4.2 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.2
aws ecr get-login-password --region eu-west-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.2

subtopics.title: Writing a small, safe Dockerfile
subtopics.body:
A good Dockerfile starts from a slim base image, copies the dependency list before the application code (so the slow install step stays cached), and runs as a non-root user.

A multi-stage build uses two or more FROM lines. The first stage has compilers and build tools and produces the finished dependencies. The final stage copies only those results into a clean, small image. Smaller images download faster, start faster and give attackers fewer tools to use.

Never copy secrets such as .env files or API keys into an image. Anyone who can pull the image can read them. Add a .dockerignore file to keep them and other clutter out.
subtopics.example: Your first image for Crestline Freight was 1.9 GB because it included build tools and the test data folder. With a multi-stage build and a .dockerignore it drops to a few hundred megabytes, and a code-only change rebuilds in seconds because the dependency layer is cached.
subtopics.code:
# ---- stage 1: build dependencies ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install --upgrade pip
COPY requirements.txt .
# Install into a separate folder we can copy later
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ---- stage 2: small runtime image ----
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local          # only the installed packages
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser                                   # do not run as root
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

subtopics.title: Kubernetes: Deployment and Service
subtopics.body:
Kubernetes works from desired state. You write YAML files that describe what you want, apply them, and Kubernetes keeps adjusting reality to match.

A Pod is the smallest unit: one or more containers that run together. You rarely create pods directly. A Deployment says how many identical pods (replicas) to run and which image to use. If a pod dies, the Deployment creates a replacement.

Pods get new IP addresses whenever they are replaced, so other services need a stable way to reach them. A Service provides one stable name and address and load-balances across all healthy pods that match its label selector. Inside the cluster, other apps can simply call http://claims-api. This is called service discovery.
subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual wants the claims API to survive a server failure. You set replicas: 3. When one node goes down, Kubernetes notices within about a minute and starts a new pod on another node, while the Service keeps sending requests to the two healthy pods.
subtopics.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: claims-api
spec:
  replicas: 3                          # keep 3 copies running
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: claims-api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: claims-api}        # the Service finds pods by this label
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.2
          ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: claims-api                     # other pods call http://claims-api
spec:
  selector: {app: claims-api}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8000}]

subtopics.title: Configuration, secrets and storage
subtopics.body:
The same image should run in test and production, so settings must come from outside the image. A ConfigMap holds non-secret settings such as a log level or a model name. A Secret holds sensitive values such as database passwords. Both can be injected into containers as environment variables or files.

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, which is an encoding and offers no protection by itself. Many customers require a cloud secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) synced into the cluster, and encryption at rest turned on.

Most API pods should be stateless: they keep nothing important on local disk. When something does need its own disk, such as a database or a vector store, you use a StatefulSet with a volume mount. StatefulSets give each pod a stable name and its own persistent volume that survives restarts.
subtopics.example: The claims API needs LOG_LEVEL=info, MODEL_NAME and a DATABASE_URL with a password. The first two go into a ConfigMap. The database URL goes into a Secret created from the insurer's secret manager, so the password never appears in git or in the image.
subtopics.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: claims-config}
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  MODEL_NAME: "MODEL"
---
# Usually created by a secrets operator, never committed with real values
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: claims-secrets}
type: Opaque
stringData:
  DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://app:CHANGE_ME@db:5432/claims"
---
# In the Deployment's container spec:
#   envFrom:
#     - configMapRef: {name: claims-config}

subtopics.title: Health probes, resources and autoscaling
subtopics.body:
Kubernetes needs to know whether each pod is healthy. A readiness probe answers 'can this pod take traffic right now?'. Until it passes, the Service sends it nothing, which matters when your app spends 40 seconds loading a model. A liveness probe answers 'is this pod stuck?'. If it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes restarts the container.

Resource requests tell the scheduler how much CPU and memory a pod needs so it lands on a node with room. Limits cap how much it may use. A pod that exceeds its memory limit is killed, which shows up as OOMKilled.

A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) adds or removes replicas based on a metric such as average CPU use. This lets a service handle a Monday-morning spike without paying for peak capacity all week.
subtopics.example: Crestline's tracking API averages 30 percent CPU but hits 90 percent every weekday at 9 a.m. With an HPA targeting 60 percent CPU between 3 and 10 replicas, it grows to about 7 pods during the rush and shrinks back to 3 by noon.
subtopics.code:
# Inside the Deployment's container spec
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 3
resources:
  requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi"}   # 250m = a quarter of a CPU core
  limits:   {memory: "1Gi"}
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: tracking-api}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: tracking-api}
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}}

subtopics.title: Ingress, rollouts and rollbacks
subtopics.body:
A Service is reachable inside the cluster. To accept traffic from outside, you usually add an Ingress: a set of HTTP routing rules (hostnames, paths, TLS certificates) handled by an ingress controller such as NGINX or a cloud load balancer. Newer clusters may use the Gateway API instead, which serves the same purpose with more features.

To release a new version you change the image tag in the Deployment. By default Kubernetes performs a rolling update: it starts new pods, waits for their readiness probes, then removes old ones, so users see no downtime.

If the new version is broken, kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version in one command. Database schema changes must be backward compatible, because old and new pods run side by side during the rollout.
subtopics.example: You release claims-api 1.4.3 at 14:00. At 14:06 error rates climb because a new field is missing in production data. You run kubectl rollout undo and by 14:08 all pods are back on 1.4.2. You then fix the bug, add a test and release 1.4.4 the next morning.
subtopics.code:
# Release a new version by changing the image tag
kubectl set image deployment/claims-api \
  api=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/claims-api:1.4.3

# Watch the rolling update progress
kubectl rollout status deployment/claims-api

# Something is wrong: inspect, then roll back
kubectl get pods -l app=claims-api
kubectl logs deployment/claims-api --since=10m
kubectl rollout undo deployment/claims-api

# See the revision history
kubectl rollout history deployment/claims-api

cloud.plain: A cloud provider such as AWS, Google Cloud (GCP) or Microsoft Azure rents you computers, storage, databases and networks that you create on demand through an API instead of buying hardware. The core building blocks are the same everywhere: a private network (on AWS called a VPC, Virtual Private Cloud), permissions that say who may do what (IAM, Identity and Access Management), and entry points that let the outside world reach your service, such as an API gateway or load balancer. Terraform is a tool for describing all of this in text files, called infrastructure as code (IaC), so you can review, version and recreate it exactly.
cloud.analogy: Clicking around a cloud console is like building a house by phoning contractors one by one and hoping you remember what you asked for. Terraform is the architect's blueprint: every wall and wire is written down, anyone can review it, and you can build an identical house next door from the same drawings.
cloud.why: FDEs usually deploy inside the customer's own cloud account, where a security team must approve every network rule and permission. Handing them a Terraform plan they can read line by line is how you pass that review in days instead of months. It also means you can stand up the same stack in test, staging and production, or at a second customer, without repeating manual work.

subtopics.title: The same ideas across three clouds
subtopics.body:
Every cloud organizes resources into regions, which are geographic locations such as eu-west-1 in Ireland. Each region has several availability zones, which are separate data centers. Spreading your service across two or three zones keeps it running if one fails.

The three big providers use different names for the same concepts. Once you learn one, mapping to the others is mostly vocabulary. The table in the code block lists the most common equivalents.

Customers pick regions for legal reasons as often as technical ones. A German hospital may require that patient data never leaves an EU region. Ask about data residency in the first week.
subtopics.example: A European bank runs on Azure and a US retailer runs on AWS. For both you need a private network, a managed Postgres database, object storage for documents, a container platform and a role for your service. The architecture diagram is the same; only the resource names in your Terraform change.

Concept                 AWS                     GCP                        Azure
----------------------  ----------------------  -------------------------  ---------------------------
Private network         VPC                     VPC network                Virtual Network (VNet)
Firewall rules          Security group          Firewall rule              Network security group
Identity for a service  IAM role                Service account            Managed identity

Managed Kubernetes      EKS                     GKE                        AKS
Managed Postgres        RDS / Aurora            Cloud SQL                  Azure Database for PostgreSQL

subtopics.title: Networking: VPCs, subnets and security groups
subtopics.body:
A VPC is your own isolated network inside the cloud, defined by an IP address range written in CIDR notation, for example 10.20.0.0/16 (about 65,000 addresses). You split it into subnets, smaller ranges that live in one availability zone.

A public subnet has a route to the internet through an internet gateway. A private subnet does not. Databases and model servers belong in private subnets so nothing on the internet can reach them directly. They can still call out through a NAT gateway if the customer allows it.

A security group is a firewall attached to a resource. You list which traffic may come in, for example 'port 5432 only from the app's security group'. By default everything inbound is denied.
subtopics.example: For Riverside Health you create a VPC with two public subnets for the load balancer and two private subnets for the API pods and the database. The database security group allows port 5432 only from the API security group, so even a mistake elsewhere cannot expose patient records to the internet.

subtopics.title: IAM and least privilege
subtopics.body:
IAM controls who can do what to which resource. A policy is a document listing allowed actions (such as s3:GetObject) on specific resources (such as one bucket). A role is an identity that a service can assume to get temporary credentials, so you never store long-lived access keys in your code.

Least privilege means giving each service only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. A document search service needs to read one bucket. It does not need to delete buckets or read the finance team's data.

In Terraform, the aws_iam_policy_document data source lets you write policies in HCL instead of hand-written JSON, which is easier to read and review.
subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's security reviewer rejects your first draft because it grants s3:* on every bucket. You rewrite it to allow only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the claims-documents bucket. The review passes the same day.

subtopics.title: The Terraform workflow and state
subtopics.body:
Terraform has a short loop. terraform init downloads providers, the plugins that talk to AWS, GCP or Azure. terraform plan compares your code with what exists and prints what it would create, change or destroy. terraform apply makes those changes.

Terraform remembers what it created in a state file. The state maps each resource in your code to a real object in the cloud. For a team, state must live in a remote backend, such as an S3 bucket, with locking so two people cannot apply at the same time.

State files can contain secrets, so never commit them to git. Read every plan before applying, and look hardest at lines marked destroy or 'must be replaced', because replacing a database means losing its data.
subtopics.example: You change the database instance size from db.t3.medium to db.t3.large. The plan says '~ update in-place', which is safe. A colleague renames the database resource in code, and the plan says '-/+ destroy and then create replacement'. You stop, and use a moved block instead so Terraform understands it is the same database.
subtopics.code:
# One-time setup: download providers, connect to the remote state backend
terraform init

# Format and check the code
terraform fmt -recursive
terraform validate

# Preview changes and save the exact plan for review
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt    # paste into the pull request

# Apply exactly the plan that was reviewed
terraform apply tfplan

# Inspect what Terraform is tracking
terraform state list

subtopics.title: Variables, modules and environments
subtopics.body:
Hard-coded values make code hard to reuse. Terraform variables let you pass in values such as the region, instance size or environment name. Outputs expose values, such as a load balancer URL, for other code or people to use.

A module is a folder of Terraform files you can call like a function, with inputs and outputs. You might write one 'ai_service' module that creates the network rules, role and database for a service, then call it once for staging and once for production with different sizes.

Keep each environment's state separate, for example in a different backend key or a different cloud account, so a mistake in staging cannot touch production.
subtopics.example: Crestline Freight wants a staging copy of the tracking stack. You call the same module twice: staging with a small database and 2 replicas, production with a larger database, 3 replicas and deletion protection on. The two stacks stay identical in shape, so what worked in staging is what ships.

subtopics.title: Air-gapped deployments and Apollo
subtopics.body:
An air-gapped environment has no connection to the internet. Defense agencies, intelligence services and some banks and utilities run systems this way. You cannot pip install, pull from Docker Hub or call a hosted model API.

Palantir built a platform called Apollo to deliver and continuously update its software across many customer environments, including disconnected and classified ones. The general lesson for any FDE: treat every release as a self-contained, versioned bundle, and automate installing and upgrading it so it does not depend on an engineer typing commands on site.

In practice that means mirroring container images into the customer's internal registry, vendoring Python packages and Terraform providers, shipping model weights as files, verifying checksums or signatures, and writing a tested offline install and rollback procedure.
subtopics.example: A defense customer runs an isolated Kubernetes cluster. You prepare release 2.3.0 as a single archive with container images, a Helm chart, Python wheels and model weights, plus a SHA-256 checksum list. Their operators carry it across on approved media, verify the checksums, load images into their Harbor registry and run the install script.
subtopics.code:
# On a connected build machine: bundle everything for release 2.3.0
mkdir -p bundle/images bundle/wheels bundle/models
docker pull registry.example.com/claims-api:2.3.0
docker save registry.example.com/claims-api:2.3.0 -o bundle/images/claims-api.tar
pip download -r requirements.txt -d bundle/wheels     # offline Python packages
cp -r models/reranker-v4 bundle/models/
(cd bundle && find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} \; > SHA256SUMS)
tar czf release-2.3.0.tgz bundle

# Inside the air-gapped site
tar xzf release-2.3.0.tgz && cd bundle
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS                              # verify nothing changed
docker load -i images/claims-api.tar
docker tag registry.example.com/claims-api:2.3.0 harbor.internal/ai/claims-api:2.3.0
docker push harbor.internal/ai/claims-api:2.3.0

transformer.plain: A transformer is the neural network design behind nearly every modern large language model (LLM), such as GPT, Claude and Llama. It reads text as tokens (small chunks of text, often parts of words), turns each token into a list of numbers called an embedding, and then passes those lists through many identical layers. In each layer an attention step lets every token pull in information from other tokens, and a feed-forward step processes each token on its own. At the end, the model outputs a probability for every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats.
transformer.analogy: Picture a meeting where each person (token) holds a card with notes. In every round, each person asks a question, listens most closely to the people whose cards best answer it, and updates their own notes. After dozens of rounds, the last person's notes are good enough to guess the next word of the sentence.
transformer.why: Customers will ask why a 100-page contract costs more and responds slower than a short email, why the model misreads long part numbers, or why their Japanese documents burn through the budget. Those answers come straight from how tokens, attention and generation work. Knowing the internals also helps you choose between an embedding model and a chat model, and explain limits honestly.

subtopics.title: Tokens and Byte-Pair Encoding
subtopics.body:
Models do not read letters or whole words. A tokenizer splits text into tokens from a fixed vocabulary, often 30,000 to 200,000 entries. Each token has an integer id.

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds that vocabulary. It starts with single bytes, finds the pair of symbols that appears together most often in a large training text, merges it into a new symbol, and repeats thousands of times. Common words become one token. Rare words, long numbers, code and many non-English scripts split into several.

This matters in practice. Price, context limits and speed are all counted in tokens. The same meaning can cost noticeably more tokens in some languages than in English, and a serial number like X7-99A-2231 may split into many tokens, which can make copying it exactly less reliable.
subtopics.example: A logistics customer sends 40,000 shipping notes per day, averaging 120 English words each. As a rough rule, English runs around 1.3 tokens per word, so that is about 156 tokens per note or roughly 6.2 million input tokens per day. Their notes in Thai may use more tokens per word, so you measure with the real tokenizer before quoting costs.

subtopics.title: Embeddings and similarity
subtopics.body:
An embedding is a vector, a list of numbers such as 1,024 values, that represents a token or a whole passage. Training arranges these vectors so that similar meanings end up close together.

Three measures of closeness are common. Dot product multiplies matching positions and adds them up; it is larger when vectors point the same way and when they are long. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by both lengths, so it compares direction only and ranges from -1 to 1. Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance between the two points; smaller means more similar.

If vectors are normalized to length 1, cosine and dot product give the same ranking. Embedding models built for search (used in RAG, retrieval-augmented generation) output one vector per passage. Inside a chat model, every token has its own vector at every layer; those internal states are a different thing.
subtopics.example: A bank's help center has articles on 'reset online banking password' and 'report a lost card'. A customer types 'I forgot my login'. Its embedding has a cosine similarity of perhaps 0.82 with the password article and 0.31 with the lost card article, so search returns the password article first.
subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.3])      # "reset online banking password"
b = np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.25])     # "I forgot my login"
c = np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.0])      # "report a lost card"

def cosine(x, y):
    return x @ y / (np.linalg.norm(x) * np.linalg.norm(y))

for name, v in [("password", a), ("lost card", c)]:
    print(name,
          "dot=%.3f" % (b @ v),                    # includes length
          "cos=%.3f" % cosine(b, v),               # direction only
          "euclid=%.3f" % np.linalg.norm(b - v))   # smaller = closer

# After normalizing to length 1, dot product and cosine rank identically
b_n, a_n = b / np.linalg.norm(b), a / np.linalg.norm(a)
print(np.isclose(b_n @ a_n, cosine(b, a)))        # True

subtopics.title: Self-attention step by step
subtopics.body:
Attention lets each token decide which other tokens matter for it. Every token's vector is multiplied by three learned weight matrices to produce a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I offer?) and a value (what information do I pass on?).

The score between two tokens is the dot product of one token's query with the other's key. Scores are divided by the square root of the key size, d_k, which keeps them from growing so large that softmax, the function that turns scores into weights summing to 1, becomes all-or-nothing.

In a decoder model such as GPT or Claude, a causal mask sets scores for future tokens to minus infinity so each token only sees earlier ones. Each token's output is the weighted average of the values. Because every token compares with every other, the work grows with the square of the sequence length.
subtopics.example: In 'The claim was denied because it was late', the token 'it' should attend strongly to 'claim'. With a trained model, the attention weight from 'it' to 'claim' might be 0.6 while most other words get small weights, so the output vector for 'it' carries meaning from 'claim'.
subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)       # numerical stability
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

T, d_model, d_k = 4, 8, 8                         # 4 tokens
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x  = rng.normal(size=(T, d_model))                # token vectors
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_k)) for _ in range(3))

Q, K, V = x @ Wq, x @ Wk, x @ Wv
scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)                   # (T, T) similarity grid
mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1) * -1e9       # hide future tokens
weights = softmax(scores + mask)                  # each row sums to 1
out = weights @ V                                 # weighted mix of values

print(np.round(weights, 2))   # upper-right triangle is 0: causal

subtopics.title: Multiple heads and word order
subtopics.body:
One attention pattern cannot capture everything. Multi-head attention runs several attention computations in parallel, each with its own smaller Q, K and V matrices. One head might link pronouns to nouns, another might track which number belongs to which field. Their outputs are joined and passed through one more matrix.

Attention on its own has no idea of word order: shuffling the tokens would give the same scores. Positional encodings fix this. The original transformer added fixed sine and cosine patterns to the embeddings (absolute positions). Relative schemes instead encode the distance between two tokens.

Most current open models use RoPE, rotary position embeddings. RoPE rotates pairs of numbers in each query and key by an angle that depends on position. The dot product between two rotated vectors then depends on how far apart the tokens are, which is exactly the relative information attention needs.
subtopics.example: In 'refund 45 after 30 days' versus 'refund 30 after 45 days', the tokens are the same but the meaning differs. Without positional information, attention would treat both identically. With RoPE, the query from 'after' lines up differently with each number depending on where it sits.
subtopics.code:
import numpy as np

def rope(x: np.ndarray, base: float = 10000.0) -> np.ndarray:
    # x: (T, d) with d even. Rotate each pair of dims by a position-dependent angle.
    T, d = x.shape
    pos = np.arange(T)[:, None]                        # (T, 1)
    freqs = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)          # (d/2,) slower for later pairs
    angle = pos * freqs                                # (T, d/2)
    cos, sin = np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0::2], x[:, 1::2]                    # split into pairs
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[:, 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin                 # 2D rotation
    out[:, 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out

q = np.ones((5, 8))
r = rope(q)
# Same vector at different positions now differs, but lengths are unchanged
print(np.round(np.linalg.norm(r, axis=1), 3))       # all equal

subtopics.title: Residuals, RMSNorm and feed-forward
subtopics.body:
A transformer layer has two sub-blocks: attention, then a feed-forward network (FFN). The FFN is a small two-layer neural network applied to each token independently. It widens the vector (often around 4 times), applies a non-linear function, then shrinks it back. Much of the model's learned knowledge is thought to live in these weights.

Each sub-block is wrapped in a residual connection: its output is added to its input instead of replacing it. This gives information and training signals a direct path through dozens of layers.

Before each sub-block, a normalization step keeps numbers in a stable range. Many modern models use RMSNorm, which divides a vector by its root mean square and multiplies by learned scales. It is simpler and cheaper than the older LayerNorm, which also subtracts the mean. Models then stack this layer N times, for example 32 or 80.
subtopics.example: Think of residuals as tracked changes in a document. Each layer proposes edits on top of the current text instead of rewriting it from scratch. After 40 layers of edits, the vector for the last token has been refined to predict the next word, while early information is still available.

subtopics.title: Model families and generation cost
subtopics.body:
There are three main families. Encoder-only models such as BERT let every token see every other token in both directions. They are good at understanding tasks: classification and producing embeddings. Decoder-only models such as GPT, Claude and Llama use the causal mask and generate text one token at a time. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 read the input with an encoder and write the output with a decoder, a design that suits translation and summarization.

Generating has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once, in parallel. Decode then produces output tokens one by one. Each new token needs the keys and values of all earlier tokens, so servers keep them in a KV cache instead of recomputing them. Long prompts make prefill slower and the KV cache larger, and output length drives decode time.

Cost follows the same shape: providers usually charge per input token and a higher price per output token, and many offer discounts for reusing a cached prompt prefix.
subtopics.example: A legal team wants to summarize 200 contracts per day, each 30,000 tokens, into 800-token summaries. That is 6 million input tokens and 160,000 output tokens daily. Because the instructions and examples are the same for every contract, putting them first and enabling prompt caching reduces repeated input cost. Latency per contract is dominated by prefill on the long input plus decoding 800 tokens.
subtopics.code:
# Rough daily cost and latency estimator. Prices are placeholders:
# look up your provider's current per-million-token rates.
PRICE_IN_PER_M  = 3.00     # $ per 1M input tokens  (placeholder)
PRICE_OUT_PER_M = 15.00    # $ per 1M output tokens (placeholder)

docs_per_day   = 200
input_tokens   = 30_000     # per contract
output_tokens  = 800        # per summary
decode_tps     = 60         # output tokens per second (measure yours)

daily_in  = docs_per_day * input_tokens
daily_out = docs_per_day * output_tokens
cost = daily_in / 1e6 * PRICE_IN_PER_M + daily_out / 1e6 * PRICE_OUT_PER_M

print(f"input tokens/day : {daily_in:,}")
print(f"output tokens/day: {daily_out:,}")
print(f"est. cost/day    : ${cost:,.2f}")
print(f"decode time/doc  : ~{output_tokens / decode_tps:.0f}s plus prefill")

glossary: Token
A chunk of text, often a word piece, with an integer id in the model's vocabulary.
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
A tokenizer training method that repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pair.
Embedding
A vector of numbers representing a token or passage so that similar meanings are close together.
Query, key, value
Three vectors per token used by attention: what it looks for, what it offers, and what it passes on.
Softmax
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
Causal mask
A mask that prevents each token from attending to later tokens during generation.
RoPE
Rotary position embeddings: rotating queries and keys by position so attention reflects relative distance.
Residual connection
Adding a sub-block's output to its input so information passes through deep networks.
RMSNorm
A normalization that divides a vector by its root mean square and applies a learned scale.
KV cache
Stored keys and values of earlier tokens so each new token does not recompute them.

Deliverable: a small table of tokens per word and one paragraph on what it means for cost.

Extend the numpy attention example to two heads with d_k = 4 each, concatenate their outputs and project with a 8x8 matrix. Deliverable: the code and a printout of both heads' attention weight matrices.
