context.plain: The context is everything a language model receives on a single call: the instructions, the conversation so far, documents you retrieved, the list of tools it may use and their results, facts about the user, and the output format you want. Context engineering is the practice of deciding what goes into that input, in what order and within what size limit. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can take in at once. A model has no memory between calls beyond what you put back into its context, so the quality of its answer depends heavily on the quality of what you assemble.
context.analogy: Think of the model as a very capable temp worker who starts each task with amnesia. Everything they know about your case is in the folder you hand them. A thin folder leads to guesses, and a folder stuffed with 500 irrelevant pages leads to missed details. Context engineering is preparing the right folder every time.
context.why: When a customer's agent gives a wrong answer, their first instinct is to tweak the prompt wording. In production, the cause is more often that the relevant policy was never retrieved, a tool returned 40,000 tokens of noise, or old chat history pushed out the key fact. An FDE who can inspect and fix the assembled context resolves these issues quickly and can explain the fix to the customer.

subtopics.title: Vibe coding, prompts and context
subtopics.body:
Vibe coding is building by feel: you ask a model for something, look at the result, and keep nudging until it seems right. It is fast for prototypes and fragile for production because nothing is measured.

Prompt engineering focuses on the wording of instructions: role descriptions, examples, step-by-step directions. It still matters, but it only covers one part of the input.

Context engineering treats the whole input as a system you design. It asks where each piece comes from, how much space it gets, how it is ordered, how it is refreshed as a conversation goes on, and how you will debug it. It is closer to software engineering than to copywriting.
subtopics.example: A retailer's returns assistant keeps approving returns outside the 30-day window. The vibe fix is adding 'be careful about dates!' to the prompt. The context fix is noticing the order date was never passed in, adding a get_order tool whose result includes order_date and today's date, and writing an evaluation case for day 31.
subtopics.code:
Symptom: assistant approved a return on day 41.

Vibe coding        -> "try again, be stricter"           (no record, no test)
Prompt engineering -> add rule: "Returns allowed within 30 days"
Context engineering-> ask: what did the model actually see?
   [x] instructions contained the 30-day rule
   [ ] order_date present?            -> NO, missing
   [ ] today's date present?          -> NO, missing
   Fix: add get_order tool + inject current date in user state
   Test: eval case 'order placed 41 days ago' expects refusal

subtopics.title: The window as RAM and a token budget
subtopics.body:
Andrej Karpathy popularized a helpful comparison: the LLM is like a CPU and its context window is like RAM. The model can only work with what is currently loaded. The space is finite, and everything you add competes with everything else.

A bigger window does not remove the problem. Cost and latency grow with input tokens, and research on long contexts has shown that models often use information in the middle of a long input less reliably than information near the start or end.

So set a budget. Decide roughly how many tokens each component may use, measure actual usage on every call, and trim the biggest offenders first. The Anthropic SDK has a count_tokens method that tells you the size of a request before you send it.
subtopics.example: An insurer's claims agent has a 200,000-token window but averages 140,000 tokens per call because it includes every document attached to a claim. After setting a budget of 40,000 tokens and retrieving only the top relevant sections, cost per call falls to under a third and answer accuracy on their test set goes up.
subtopics.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
MODEL = "MODEL"   # placeholder model name

system = "You are a claims assistant for Harbor Mutual. Cite sources by id."
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Why was claim C-55120 denied?\n\n" + retrieved_text}]

count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model=MODEL, system=system, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS,
)
print("input tokens:", count.input_tokens)

BUDGET = 40_000
if count.input_tokens > BUDGET:
    # Trim the biggest component first, e.g. keep fewer retrieved chunks
    retrieved_text = "\n\n".join(chunks[:3])

subtopics.title: Assembling the components
subtopics.body:
A typical context has six parts. Instructions describe the role, rules and tone. Dialogue history holds earlier turns. Retrieved chunks (RAG) are passages from documents found by search. Tool schemas describe the functions the model may call, and tool outputs are what those calls returned. User state holds facts about who is asking, such as role, region and permissions. Output constraints describe the exact format you will parse.

Order and labeling help. Put stable instructions first, which also allows prompt caching of that prefix. Wrap retrieved material in clear tags with source ids so the model can cite it and you can trace it. Put the user's actual question near the end.

Only include what this call needs. If the user is a branch employee, do not load tools meant for administrators, and do not retrieve documents they are not allowed to see.
subtopics.example: For a bank's internal policy assistant, a teller in Ohio asks about wire transfer limits. The context includes the policy instructions, the last 4 turns, 3 retrieved policy sections with ids, one lookup_limit tool, the user state (role teller, state OH) and a rule to answer in under 120 words with citations.
subtopics.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
MODEL = "MODEL"

tools = [{
    "name": "lookup_limit",
    "description": "Return the wire transfer limit for a role and US state.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
        "properties": {"role": {"type": "string"}, "state": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["role", "state"]},
}]

system = ("You answer questions about Acme Bank internal policy. "
          "Use only the documents provided. Cite ids like [POL-12]. "
          "If the answer is not in the documents, say you don't know. "
          "Answer in under 120 words.")

docs = "\n".join(f'<doc id="{c.id}">{c.text}</doc>' for c in top_chunks)
user_state = "<user role='teller' state='OH' />"

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=500, system=system, tools=tools,
    messages=history[-8:] + [{"role": "user",
        "content": f"{user_state}\n<documents>\n{docs}\n</documents>\n\n{question}"}],
)

subtopics.title: Managing history and tool outputs
subtopics.body:
Conversations and agent runs grow with every turn. If you append everything forever, the window fills with old chatter and bulky tool results, and the important facts get crowded out.

A common pattern is to keep the most recent turns word for word and replace older ones with a running summary. The summary should keep decisions, facts and open questions, and drop small talk.

Tool outputs deserve the same care. An API might return a 30 KB JSON object when the model needs five fields. Trim it before adding it to the context, and keep the full result in your logs in case you need it later.
subtopics.example: A field-service agent for an energy company runs 25 tool calls to diagnose a turbine fault. Raw outputs total 90,000 tokens. By keeping only fields such as sensor_id, reading, unit and timestamp, and summarizing turns older than the last six, each call stays under 20,000 tokens and the agent stops forgetting the fault code it found early on.

subtopics.title: Context as a compiler
subtopics.body:
A useful mental model is to treat the assembled context as source code and the model as a compiler. The same compiler produces a working or broken program depending on the source you feed it. Likewise, the same model produces a correct or wrong answer depending on the context.

This framing pushes you toward engineering habits. Build the context with code in one function, not by string concatenation scattered across the app. Version it. Log the exact context and the output for every call, with a request id, so you can reproduce any answer later.

Once contexts are logged, you can diff them. When an answer changes between Tuesday and Wednesday, compare the two contexts line by line. Usually the difference explains the behavior.
subtopics.example: A hospital's discharge assistant suddenly starts omitting medication changes. Diffing the logged contexts shows a retrieval configuration change on Tuesday reduced chunks from 5 to 2, which dropped the pharmacy notes. Reverting it fixes the issue without touching the prompt.
subtopics.code:
import hashlib, json, time, uuid

def build_context(question, user, history, chunks, tools) -> dict:
    # Single place where context is assembled: easy to version and test
    return {
        "version": "ctx-v7",
        "system": SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        "tools": [t["name"] for t in tools],
        "user_state": {"role": user.role, "region": user.region},
        "chunks": [{"id": c.id, "score": round(c.score, 3)} for c in chunks],
        "messages": history + [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    }

def log_call(ctx: dict, output: str) -> str:
    rid = str(uuid.uuid4())
    record = {"request_id": rid, "ts": time.time(), "context": ctx, "output": output,
              "ctx_hash": hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(ctx, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()}
    with open("context_log.jsonl", "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")
    return rid

subtopics.title: Debugging hallucinations like runtime errors
subtopics.body:
A hallucination is an answer that sounds confident but is not supported by facts. In production, it helps to treat one like a runtime error with a cause you can find.

Work through a fixed checklist. First, was the needed fact in the context at all? If not, fix retrieval or tool access. Second, was it there but buried among many irrelevant chunks? Rerank and trim. Third, was it there but contradicted by stale content? Remove or date-filter the old source. Fourth, did the instructions allow the model to say 'I don't know'? If not, add that.

Finally, turn every fixed bug into an evaluation case: a saved question with the expected answer or behavior, run automatically before each release. Over time this set becomes the customer's proof that the system is improving.
subtopics.example: Harbor Mutual's agent tells a policyholder that flood damage is covered. Checking the log shows the flood exclusion clause was chunk 9 of 10 retrieved and a 2019 marketing page saying 'we cover you in every storm' was chunk 1. You exclude marketing pages from the index, add a reranker, and add the case to the evaluation set with the expected answer 'not covered, see clause 4.2'.
subtopics.code:
def diagnose(record: dict, must_contain: str) -> str:
    ctx_text = json.dumps(record["context"]).lower()
    if must_contain.lower() not in ctx_text:
        return "MISSING: fact not in context -> fix retrieval or tools"
    chunk_ids = [c["id"] for c in record["context"]["chunks"]]
    if len(chunk_ids) > 6:
        return "BURIED: fact present among many chunks -> rerank and trim"
    return "PRESENT: check for conflicting sources and 'I don't know' rule"

# Regression evals built from real failures
EVALS = [
    {"q": "Is flood damage covered under policy HM-Home-2?", "expect": "not covered"},
    {"q": "Can I return an item after 41 days?",               "expect": "no"},
]

def run_evals(answer_fn):
    fails = [e for e in EVALS if e["expect"] not in answer_fn(e["q"]).lower()]
    print(f"{len(EVALS) - len(fails)}/{len(EVALS)} passed")
    return fails

glossary: Context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can read in one call, including instructions and history.
Context engineering
Designing and assembling everything the model sees on each call, within a token budget.
Prompt engineering
Crafting the wording of instructions and examples given to a model.
RAG
Retrieval-augmented generation: searching documents and adding the best passages to the context.
Tool schema
A structured description of a function the model may call, including its name and parameters.
Token budget
A planned limit on how many tokens each part of the context may use.
Prompt caching
Reusing the processed form of an unchanged prompt prefix to cut cost and latency.
Hallucination
A fluent, confident answer that is not supported by the provided facts or reality.
Evaluation set
A saved collection of test questions and expected behaviors run before each release.
practice: Take any chatbot prompt you have written and break its full input into the six components (instructions, history, retrieved docs, tools, user state, output format). Deliverable: a context budget table with token counts for each, measured with a tokenizer or count_tokens.

Build a small Q&A script over 20 documents of your choice that logs the full assembled context and output to a JSONL file for every call. Deliverable: the script and one logged record with a wrong answer, annotated with the cause you found.

Stretch: create 15 evaluation questions for your Q&A script, then improve context assembly (reranking, trimming, 'I don't know' rule) without changing the model. Deliverable: before and after pass rates and a short note on which change helped most.

ace.plain: Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) is a method, described by researchers from Stanford and collaborators in 2025, for letting an AI agent improve over time by updating its context instead of retraining the model. The context is kept as a playbook: a growing list of short, specific lessons, each with an id and counters for how often it helped or hurt. Three roles cooperate: a Generator does the task, a Reflector studies what happened and extracts lessons, and a Curator merges those lessons into the playbook as small edits called delta updates. Because edits are small and itemized, useful details are kept instead of being summarized away.
ace.analogy: Think of a hospital ward's shared handbook. A nurse does the shift (Generator), a senior nurse reviews incidents afterward (Reflector), and the ward manager adds or amends individual numbered entries in the handbook (Curator). Nobody rewrites the whole handbook from memory each week, which is how hard-won details would get lost.
ace.why: Customers want their agents to get better from real use without a fine-tuning project each month. An FDE deploying a support or data agent can log its runs, turn failures into playbook entries, and show measurable improvement in weeks. Understanding ACE also helps you avoid a common mistake: having a model rewrite its own long system prompt every iteration until it becomes vague and loses the details that made it work.

subtopics.title: Two failure modes: brevity bias and collapse
subtopics.body:
Many automatic prompt-improvement methods ask a model to rewrite the prompt to be better. Two problems show up.

Brevity bias is the tendency of these optimizers to produce short, generic instructions. 'Be careful with dates' is short and sounds wise, but it drops the specific fact that one vendor sends dates as day/month. Domain detail is exactly what agents need, and it is the first thing a summary removes.

Context collapse happens when a model rewrites the entire accumulated context at each step. Each rewrite loses a bit, and over many rounds the context can shrink sharply and performance drops. The ACE authors describe this effect and design around it.
subtopics.example: A finance team's agent learns over two weeks that invoice API pages use cursors, that vendor Alpha sends DD/MM dates, and that refunds need a manager id. A monolithic rewrite on day 15 condenses 2,400 words of learned notes into 150 words of general advice. The next day, three previously fixed bugs return.
subtopics.code:
Day 14 context (itemized, detailed)          Day 15 after full rewrite
-------------------------------------        ---------------------------
- Invoice API: use cursor, not offset         - Handle APIs carefully.
- Vendor Alpha dates are DD/MM                - Validate dates.
- Vendor Beta dates are MM/DD                 - Follow approval rules.
- Refunds > $500 need manager_id
- On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After header
- Currency field is minor units (cents)
  ... 40 more specific lessons ...

Result: brevity bias + context collapse -> old bugs return.
ACE's answer: never rewrite the whole thing; apply small itemized edits.

subtopics.title: The playbook as structured data
subtopics.body:
In ACE the context is a list of bullets, each a self-contained lesson. Each bullet has an id, a section (such as strategies, common errors or tool tips), the text, and counters for how many times it was marked helpful or harmful.

Storing the playbook as data, instead of one big block of text, makes it easy to add, update, remove or rank individual items. You can render it into the prompt for the Generator, and you can edit it with ordinary code.

Counters give you a feedback signal. A bullet that keeps being marked harmful should be revised or removed. A bullet that is often helpful can be placed earlier.
subtopics.example: For Northwind's data agent the playbook has 38 bullets. Bullet err-004 says 'Vendor feed dates are DD/MM; parse explicitly' with helpful=3 and harmful=1, because it broke once on a US vendor. That signal prompts the Curator to split it into two vendor-specific bullets.

subtopics.title: The Generator and its trajectory
subtopics.body:
The Generator is the agent that does the actual work. It receives the task and the rendered playbook as part of its context, then reasons, calls tools and produces an answer.

Everything it does is recorded as a trajectory: the sequence of reasoning steps, tool calls, tool results and the final outcome. The trajectory also records which playbook bullets the Generator said it used.

Feedback can come from ground-truth labels, but ACE is designed to also work with execution feedback: whether code ran, whether an API call succeeded, whether tests passed. This matters in customer settings, where labeled answers are often scarce but logs of success and failure are plentiful.
subtopics.example: Task: 'Total unpaid invoices for vendor Beta in March'. The Generator uses bullet str-012 to page with a cursor, but parses Beta's dates as DD/MM because of bullet err-004. The SQL returns 0 rows for March, and a sanity check comparing to the vendor's statement fails. That failed trajectory is exactly what the Reflector needs.
subtopics.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
MODEL = "MODEL"

def generate(task: str, playbook: Playbook, tools: list) -> dict:
    system = ("You are a finance data agent. Use the playbook below. "
              "At the end, list the bullet ids you relied on as USED: [ids].\n\n"
              + playbook.render())
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    trajectory = []
    while True:
        resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=2000,
                                      system=system, tools=tools, messages=messages)
        trajectory.append(resp.model_dump())             # record every step
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            break
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        results = [run_tool(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # tool_result blocks
        trajectory.append({"tool_results": results})
    return {"task": task, "trajectory": trajectory, "final": resp.content}

subtopics.title: The Reflector extracts lessons
subtopics.body:
The Reflector is a separate model call whose only job is analysis. It reads the trajectory and the feedback and answers: what went wrong, what was the root cause, what should be done differently, and which existing bullets helped or hurt.

Keeping reflection separate from generation helps. The Generator is focused on finishing the task. A separate reviewer with a clear brief tends to produce more specific, honest diagnoses. The ACE work also allows the Reflector to refine its lessons over more than one pass.

Ask for structured output, such as JSON, so the next stage can process it with code. Push for concrete, reusable lessons that name the vendor, the field and the fix.
subtopics.example: Given the failed Beta invoice run, the Reflector returns: root cause 'Beta uses MM/DD dates, err-004 assumes DD/MM for all vendors'; new lesson 'Vendor Beta dates are MM/DD; check vendor before parsing'; tags err-004 as harmful and str-012 as helpful.
subtopics.code:
import json

REFLECT_PROMPT = """You review an agent's run. Return JSON only:
{"root_cause": str,
 "lessons": [{"section": "strategies|errors|tools", "text": str}],
 "bullet_tags": [{"id": str, "tag": "helpful|harmful|neutral"}]}
Lessons must be specific and reusable: name systems, fields and fixes."""

def reflect(run: dict, feedback: str) -> dict:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, max_tokens=1500, system=REFLECT_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"TASK: {run['task']}\nFEEDBACK: {feedback}\n"
            f"TRAJECTORY:\n{json.dumps(run['trajectory'])[:50000]}"}],
    )
    return json.loads(resp.content[0].text)   # validate in production

subtopics.title: The Curator applies delta updates
subtopics.body:
The Curator turns the Reflector's output into small edits to the playbook. A delta is a list of operations: add a new bullet, update counters on an existing bullet, or occasionally revise or remove one. Nothing else in the playbook changes.

Deltas can be applied with ordinary code, so they are cheap, predictable and easy to audit. You can also batch deltas from many runs and merge them together.

The playbook would grow forever without care, so ACE uses a grow-and-refine approach: new bullets are added, and periodically near-duplicates are merged (for example by comparing embeddings) and consistently harmful bullets are pruned. For a customer deployment, also gate new bullets behind your evaluation set before they go live.
subtopics.example: From the Beta failure, the Curator emits two operations: add err-009 'Vendor Beta dates are MM/DD; check vendor before parsing' and increment harmful on err-004. The next Beta task succeeds. After 200 runs, a refine pass merges three near-identical retry bullets into one and removes a bullet with harmful=6, helpful=0.

subtopics.title: Measuring context management
subtopics.body:
How do you know an agent manages its context well? You need tasks where the answer must be found across several places, and you check whether the agent finds and combines the right pieces.

Letta, the company behind the open-source agent framework of the same name, published Context-Bench for this purpose. It evaluates how well models perform agentic context engineering: finding information spread across files by chaining tool calls such as grep_files (search file contents) and open_files (read a file). Tasks are multi-hop, meaning one lookup reveals what to search for next.

For your own customer work you can build a small benchmark in the same spirit: a folder of realistic documents, a set of multi-hop questions with known answers, simple file tools, and a script that scores answers and records how many tool calls and tokens each run used.
subtopics.example: For a manufacturer you create 60 documents: supplier contracts, part catalogs and incident reports. A question such as 'Which supplier made the valve that failed in incident IR-221, and what is their warranty period?' needs three hops: the incident report gives a part number, the catalog maps it to a supplier, and the contract gives the warranty. You score accuracy and average tokens per question before and after adding ACE.

glossary: ACE
Agentic Context Engineering: improving an agent by evolving an itemized context playbook through generate, reflect and curate steps.
Playbook
A structured list of specific lessons (bullets) that is rendered into the agent's context.
Generator
The ACE role that performs the task using the current playbook and records its trajectory.
Reflector
The ACE role that analyzes a trajectory and feedback to extract concrete lessons.
Curator
The ACE role that turns lessons into small itemized edits to the playbook.
Delta update
A small edit, such as adding one bullet or bumping a counter, applied instead of a full rewrite.
Brevity bias
The tendency of prompt optimizers to compress instructions into short, generic advice that loses detail.
Context collapse
The loss of detail and quality when a model repeatedly rewrites an entire context.
Trajectory
The full record of an agent run: steps, tool calls, results and outcome.
Multi-hop retrieval
Answering a question that needs several lookups, where each result guides the next search.
practice: Write a playbook of 10 bullets for an agent you know (for example a SQL helper), with ids, sections and helpful/harmful counters, stored as JSON. Deliverable: the JSON file and a render function that prints it as prompt text.

Implement the Reflector and Curator for that agent: feed it three failed runs (real or hand-written), collect the JSON reflections and apply them as deltas. Deliverable: the playbook before and after, plus a diff showing only the changed bullets.

Stretch: build a mini Context-Bench style evaluation with 30 text files, 10 multi-hop questions, and grep_files and open_files tools. Run the agent with an empty playbook, then again after 20 ACE iterations. Deliverable: accuracy, average tool calls and average tokens for both runs, and a short note on any bullet that hurt.
